opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that a number on its own hides almost everything that matters about how much you should trust it.

When a lab publishes something like "our model scored 23% on this dangerous-capabilities benchmark," you're implicitly trusting a whole chain of decisions you can't see. Did they elicit the model's capabilities properly, or did they run it with a lazy prompt and no scaffolding? Did they fine-tune for the task, or just zero-shot it? Is the benchmark contaminated? Did they pick the evaluation after seeing which ones looked good? Is the threshold they compare against meaningful, or was it set to make the model pass? Each of those can move the result enormously, sometimes from "clearly safe" to "clearly concerning," and none of it shows up in the headline number.

So a published score is really a claim of the form "trust us, we did this competently and in good faith." For a lot of these evaluations, especially the ones about whether a model could meaningfully help with something dangerous, the answer is very sensitive to elicitation effort. Under-elicitation is the default failure mode. It's easy to make a model look less capable than it is, and there's a mild incentive to do that, even without anyone intending to.

A third-party auditor addresses this directly. They can look at the setup, poke at it, try harder elicitation themselves, ask "why didn't you try X?", and then say whether the process holds up. What you get from them isn't mainly a better number. It's a judgment about whether the number means what it's claimed to mean. That's the thing outsiders actually need and can't get from a leaderboard.

There's also a structural point. A lot of the relevant information can't be published: model weights, sensitive details of bioweapons-relevant evals, internal training details. So "just publish everything and let the public check" doesn't really work for the most important evaluations. An auditor with privileged access, under confidentiality, is a way of getting independent scrutiny without releasing hazardous information.

I'd add some caveats. Auditing is only as good as the auditor's competence, access, and independence. If the auditor gets a week with a checkpoint and a restricted API, or depends commercially on staying friendly with the lab, it can turn into a rubber stamp. And I don't think quantitative scores are useless. They're great for tracking trends and comparing models under a shared methodology. But if the question is "should I trust this safety claim about this model," I'd rather have a knowledgeable, independent person tell me they really tried to break it and couldn't than a number I have no way to interpret.

r001.rationale: The response says auditors can inspect the setup and question the threshold, but it does not clearly state that inspecting evaluation examples and how they were graded is more informative than scores alone.

fable-5.1.text:
So the core issue is that a quantitative score, once it's published, becomes a target. If a lab says "our model scored 12% on our dangerous capability eval," that number is doing a lot of work, and almost none of the work is visible to the reader. What was the elicitation effort? Did they fine-tune, did they give it tools, did they let it try ten times or once? What's the threshold, and who set it, and was it set before or after they saw the result? You can produce almost any number you want by making reasonable-sounding choices on each of those questions, and the reader has no way to tell the difference between a lab that tried really hard to make the model succeed and one that ran it once with a default prompt.

And I don't even think this requires anyone to be acting in bad faith. The people running these evals are under commercial pressure, they're under time pressure, and they're also just genuinely uncertain about the right methodology. So you get a lot of judgment calls, and the judgment calls tend to drift in whichever direction is convenient. A published score flattens all of that into one number that looks far more objective than it is.

A third-party auditor can actually look at those judgment calls. They can ask, did you try harder than this? They can run their own elicitation. They can look at the transcripts rather than the summary statistic. And crucially, they can say "this evaluation was conducted competently and the conclusion is supported" without that having to be reducible to a number that then gets compared across labs in ways that don't make sense, because the evals aren't the same.

I'd also say the thing we actually care about isn't the score, it's the decision. Is this model safe to deploy, or to continue training? That's a holistic judgment. Scores are inputs to it, but if we've learned anything from benchmarks in ML generally, it's that the moment a number becomes the thing that matters, it stops measuring what you wanted it to measure. An auditor who can look at the whole process is much harder to Goodhart than a leaderboard.

Now, I don't want to oversell this. Auditing has its own problems. The auditors need deep technical expertise, which is scarce. They need real access, which labs are reluctant to give. And there's a risk of capture, where the auditor just becomes a rubber stamp. But I think those are solvable problems, whereas "the number means what you think it means" is not really a solvable problem for published scores. So I'd rather put effort into building the auditing ecosystem than into standardizing scores that will inevitably be gamed.

r001.rationale: The response says auditors can inspect transcripts and methodological judgment calls, including how thresholds were set, to assess whether the conclusion is supported; it contrasts this with relying on a summary score alone.

astra-6.text:
I think the main issue is that a quantitative score leaves out a lot of the context you need to interpret an evaluation. If a model gets a low score on a dangerous-capability evaluation, does that mean it lacks the capability, or that the evaluators didn’t find a good way to elicit it? You can’t usually tell from the number alone.

A third-party auditor can look at the process behind that number: what tests were run, how much effort went into eliciting the capability, what limitations were identified, and whether the conclusions actually follow from the evidence. They can also have access to sensitive details that you wouldn’t necessarily want published.

So I wouldn’t say quantitative scores are useless. They’re useful evidence. But what I really want is a credible, independent assessment of whether the evaluation supports the safety claim being made. Auditing can give you more of that than a published score can.

r001.rationale: The response says auditors can inspect the tests, elicitation effort, limitations, and evidence behind a conclusion. It does not specifically say that reviewing evaluation examples and how they were graded is more informative than scores alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that a quantitative score leaves out a lot of the context you need to interpret it. If a model gets a low score on an evaluation of some dangerous capability, is that because it lacks the capability, or because the people running the evaluation didn’t find a good way to elicit it? What tools did they give it? How much effort did they put into prompting it? Those details can really change what you should conclude.

A third-party auditor can look at the process behind the result. They can ask whether the tests actually address the risks we care about, whether the people running them made reasonable choices, and whether the conclusions are supported by the evidence. They can also examine information that a company might reasonably not want to publish, such as the details of how to elicit a dangerous capability.

So I’m not against publishing numbers. They can be useful evidence. But I’d put more weight on an independent party being able to scrutinize the evaluation and challenge its assumptions than on a headline score that looks comparable across companies but may have been produced under very different conditions.

r001.rationale: The response says auditors can scrutinize the evaluation process and evidence behind conclusions, but it does not state that inspecting evaluation examples and how they were graded is more informative than scores alone.
